title: Game 10: Hans vs Magnus
notes: Game 10 of 12 in the experiment, from the Caro-Kann Defence. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

Black's 4...Bf5 attacks my knight on e4, so I need to address it; Ng3 is the main-line Caro-Kann move, kicking the bishop while gaining time for h4-h5 ideas later. Alternatives like Nc5 or Nd6+ just lose time and let Black equalize easily.

My bishop on f5 is attacked by Ng3 and undefended, and both greedy options fail: 5...Bxc2 6.Qxc2 and 5...Qxd4 6.Nxf5 just lose a piece. The standard retreat 5...Bg6 keeps the bishop safe on a square where no pawn or piece can harass it, retaining the good light-squared bishop for the Caro-Kann structure.

This is the standard Caro-Kann Classical structure, and the main theoretical plan is to harass the bishop with h4-h5, gaining space on the kingside and forcing it to the passive h7 square. After 6...h6 7.h5 Bh7 8.Bd3 I get a pleasant space advantage with easy development.

This is the main-line Classical Caro-Kann; if I don't play ...h6 now, White's h5 traps my bishop on g6 since it has no pawn support or safe retreat along that diagonal. ...h6 gives the bishop the h7 escape square and keeps my development (Nf6, e6, Nbd7) flowing before any central break, and White has no checks or captures to exploit it.

This is the Caro-Kann Classical, and the main line continues 7.Nf3 developing toward Bd3 while keeping h5 in reserve to cramp the h7 bishop. Nf3 is safe — no captures or checks available for Black, and it guards the e5/g5 squares.

The d4 pawn is defended by the queen and c2 by the queen too, so Qxd4 and Bxc2 just lose material — I checked those greedy captures first. I'll follow main-line theory with 7...Nd7, developing a minor piece before any central break and preparing ...Bh7 if White plays h5.

This is the Caro-Kann Classical; the standard plan is to kick the bishop with h5, trapping it on h7 and gaining space, after which Bd3 trades off Black's good bishop and leaves me with a lasting kingside space edge. Black's bishop has only h7 available, so there's no tactical downside.

8...Bxh5 just loses a piece to 9.Nxh5, and leaving the bishop on g6 invites Nxg6 or further pawn hits, so I retreat it to the safe h7 square as in the main line, keeping my structure intact and preparing ...e6, ...Ngf6 and queenside development.

This is the main-line Classical Caro-Kann, and the standard plan is to trade off the light-squared bishop that Black has spent moves preserving. After 9. Bd3 Bxd3 10. Qxd3 I get a comfortable space advantage with the h5 wedge; alternatives like Bxh6 fail to gxh6 winning a piece for one pawn.

This is the main-line Classical Caro-Kann: my h7 bishop is passive and boxed in, and White's Bd3 offers the trade, so I take it while the recapture is forced to be with the queen (no pawn-structure damage, no open file toward my king). After 10.Qxd3 I follow with ...e6 and ...Ngf6, getting my minors out and castling before considering ...c5 or ...e5.

This is the main-line Classical Caro-Kann, and the bishop on d3 must simply be recaptured; Qxd3 develops the queen to its best square eyeing h7/b5 and keeps cxd3's structural damage off the table. Tempting alternatives like Bxh6 fail since Black just answers gxh6 with an extra piece after the d3 bishop stays, so recapture is forced in practice.

This is the main-line Classical Caro-Kann and the book move is to develop the kingside knight; 10...Ngf6 keeps the e5 square covered twice (d7-knight plus f6-knight) and prepares ...e6 and ...Be7 without any loose pieces. I rejected 10...Ne5 (11.Nxe5 simply wins a piece since nothing recaptures) and 10...e5, which opens lines against my uncastled king — my rules say finish developing before any central break.

This is the main line Caro-Kann Classical structure, and the standard plan is to develop the bishop actively and castle long. Bf4 controls e5, prepares O-O-O, and after 11...Nd5 I can retreat with Bd2 or hold with Be5; Bxh6 would just lose a piece to gxh6.

11...Nxh5 simply loses a piece to Nxh5, so I stick with the main-line developing move 11...e6, which opens my bishop, solidifies the d5/f5 squares and prepares Be7/Qa5+ and castling; I checked White's tries — 12.Ne5 Nxe5 13.dxe5 Nd5 and 12.Qb3 Qb6 lose nothing.

This is the standard Classical Caro-Kann structure, where my king belongs on the queenside behind the pawns while my h5 pawn and open h-file give me kingside pressure. Bxh6 gxh6 gives nothing concrete since Qg6 isn't check with the f7 pawn in place, so I'll follow the main line and develop with castling, keeping ideas like Ne4/Ne5 and Rh4 in reserve.

Greedy 12...Nxh5 loses material after 13.Nxh5 Rxh5 14.Rxh5, and 12...Bd6 invites 13.Bxd6 Qxd6 or 13.Ne4, easing White's attack, so I develop solidly with 12...Be7 to prepare castling and keep my structure intact. I checked White's tries: 13.Ne5 Nxe5 14.dxe5 Nd5 is fine, and 13.Ne4 Nxe4 14.Qxe4 Nf6 just gains me a tempo.

This is the Caro-Kann Classical where my position is already well-developed, so rather than committing with Ne4 (which releases tension) or Ne5 (which hands Black the d5 square after dxe5), I prefer a useful prophylactic move. Kb1 steps off the c1-h6 diagonal and the c-file before any ...Qa5/...b5 or ...Rc8 counterplay, keeping Ne5, g4 and Rde1 all available.

With the h-file half-open and White's Rh1 plus the fixed h5 pawn, castling short invites a g4-g5 storm, so I prefer the flexible main-line 13...Qc7, which develops, guards e5/d7 and keeps the option of castling queenside next to White's king where no attack exists. I checked White's tries: 14.Nf5 exf5 15.Qxf5 hits d7 but it's covered twice, 14.Ne5 Nxe5 15.dxe5 Nd5 is fine, and 14.Bxh6 gxh6 is simply a piece.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 14. Bxc7 Nd5 15. Ba5 Nf8 16. Nf5 exf5

moves.thought: Black's 13...Qc7 overlooked that my bishop on f4 controls the b8–h2 diagonal — e5 and d6 are both empty, so Bxc7 simply takes the queen, and nothing (knight on d7, rook on a8, king on e8) covers c7. That wins a queen for nothing.

My 13...Qc7 was a blunder that dropped the queen to Bxc7, so now my only priority is to win that bishop back and get my king safe. Rc8 attacks the undefended bishop on c7 along the file while still leaving kingside castling available, and I checked the recaptures: 15.Bd6 Bxd6 just loses the bishop (Qd3 is blocked by d4), 15.Bb6 axb6, and if White ignores it with 15.Qa6 I play Rxc7 and only give back the b-pawn.

I'm a full queen up after 14.Bxc7, so I just need to rescue the bishop and keep things simple; Bf4 retreats to a safe, active square (if Black tries g5 I get Bxg5 hxg5 Nxg5 winning more material). Trading with Bd6 was tempting but keeping the extra piece pressure is stronger.

I'm already down a queen for a bishop after the earlier ...Qc7 blunder, so I need safety and activity rather than more material grabs — Nxh5 just loses a knight to Nxh5 since the g3 knight guards it. Castling tucks the king away, connects the rooks and keeps Be7 covering d6 so White's queen has no entry, and I see no White check or capture on a loose piece afterwards (h6 is held by g7).

I'm already up a full queen after winning the black queen on c7, so I mainly need safe, forcing play. Bxh6 snatches another pawn and rips open the king: after gxh6 I get Qg6+ Kh8 with Rxh6+ ideas, and 16...Nxh5 17.Nxh5 gxh6 just leaves me a pawn and queen ahead. (Qh7+ is a blunder since Kxh7 simply takes the queen.)

White's bishop on h6 is completely undefended — Qd3, Nf3 and Ng3 none cover h6 — so gxh6 simply regains a piece, which is essential since I'm already down my queen after the earlier blunder. Opening the g-file is risky (17.Qg6+ Kh8 gives White play), but declining the piece leaves me hopelessly down material, and alternatives like Nxh5 only trade pieces off, which favours the side with more material.

I'm up a queen for a bishop after winning the queen on c7, so I must avoid tactics — note that Qg6+ and Qh7+ both just lose the queen (fxg6 or Kxh7), and Ng5 drops a knight to Bxg5. Instead Qe3 is completely safe (no black piece covers e3) and hits the loose h6 pawn, after which Qxh6 would support Ng5 with a real Qh7# threat.

I'm down a queen for a bishop after an earlier blunder, and h6 is simply hanging to Qe3 while my Be7 is loose, so king moves fail (17...Kg7 18.Nf5+! wins the bishop, 17...Kh7 18.Ng5+ invades) and 17...Ng4/Ne4/Ne5 all drop a piece to Qe4 or a recapture. I chose 17...Nd5, which hits the queen with tempo, is defended twice by c6 and e6, blocks the d-file, and lets me follow with ...Bf6 (guarded by the knight) to cover the dark squares and fight for the d4 pawn.

My queen on e3 is attacked by the knight on d5, so I must move it, and Qxh6 both saves the queen and grabs another pawn while keeping my attack on the exposed black king (Qxe6 fails to fxe6). I'm already up a queen for a bishop, so I just need safety: after Qxh6 Black has no tactic — Nc3+ runs into bxc3, and the queen has plenty of escape squares via g5/f4.

White is threatening h6 followed by Qg7# and also Ng5 with Qh7#, so I must cover h7 and g7 while keeping my pieces defended. 18...N5f6 guards h7 and g4, attacks h5, and is defended by both Be7 and Nd7; I keep the knight on d7 so a later Qxe6 never hits my c8 rook through the d7 square (which is why I rejected N7f6), and ...Bf6 loses a piece to Ng5.

Black's king is stripped bare and the bishop on e7 is undefended, so Nf5 hits it while creating the deadly threat of Qg7# (the queen would be protected by the knight). Black essentially must play exf5, after which Rhe1 picks up the loose bishop and my attack continues with an overwhelming material edge.

White's Nf5 covers g7, so Qg7 is immediate mate (h8, h7 and f8 all covered, f7 blocked), and nothing of mine can defend or vacate g7 in time. The only way to stop it is to remove the knight, and after exf5 the g7 square is undefended so Qg7+ Kxg7 just loses the queen; Qxf6 is met by Bxf6.

Black's king is bare on the g-file, so I want to bring the last rook into the attack with Rh4, threatening Rg4+ followed by Qg7#. The only real defence is 20...Ng4, when 21.Rxg4+ fxg4 22.Qg5+ Kh8 23.Qxe7 picks off the loose bishop (nothing defends e7) and leaves me a piece and pawns up; other tries like 20...Ne4 or 20...Nf8 simply allow Rg4+ and mate on g7.

Nf6-g4 hits the queen and f2, and I counted the chain on g4: only Rh4 attacks it while my f5 pawn defends, so 21.Rxg4+ fxg4 trades my knight for a rook and the recapture also attacks Nf3, stripping White's attackers; if White instead retreats the queen (Qg5 loses to Bxg5, Qe3 to Nxe3), my knight simply returns or trades favourably. I checked White's checks — Qg6+ Kh8 or Qh7+ (illegal/losing) give nothing lasting, and leaving f6 creates no mate since g7 and h7 are unsupported for White.

My queen on h6 is attacked by the knight on g4, so I must move it, and Qf4 does so with a double attack: it hits the knight on g4 (defended only by the f5 pawn) and the completely undefended f5 pawn itself, so Black can't hold both. Checks like Qg6+ followed by Ng5 are tempting, but after ...Bxg5 the attack simplifies, whereas Qf4 keeps all my pieces safe, keeps my big material plus, and wins another pawn.

My knight on g4 is actually safe (the f5 pawn guards g4 and e4), while White's f2 pawn is completely undefended — Qf4's file is blocked by its own Nf3 — so Nxf2 grabs a pawn and hits the loose Rd1; crucially the knight keeps the e4/g4 retreats covered by my f5 pawn. I rejected 21...Bxh4 because 22.Qxf5! double-attacks both knights (g4 and d7) and White wins a piece back, whereas after 21...Nxf2 White cannot save both d1 and h4 (22.Rd2 Bxh4 23.Qxh4/Rxf2 still leaves me winning the exchange), and 22.Qxf5 Nxd1 23.Qxd7 Bxh4 even nets me material.

Black's knight on f2 is attacking my d1 rook, so I slide it to f1 where it attacks the undefended knight instead; almost every retreat loses the knight (Ng4/Nh3 to Rh4, Nd3 to cxd3, Nd1/Nh1 to Rxd1/Rxh1). The only real try is Ne4 hitting my queen, but then Qxf5 removes its defender and forks both knights, and if Black tries Bg5 I simply take with Qxg5+.

My Nf2 is attacked by Rf1 and nothing defends it, so I must get value for it — and my Be7 sees h4, where the rook is only defended by Qf4 (through g4) and Nf3. Counting the chain, Bxh4 trades bishop for rook (+2 material for me) in every recapture; if instead I first save the knight with Ne4, White simply plays Rh3/Rh1 and keeps his extra material, and Ng4 allows Rxg4 fxg4 Qxg4+ with an attack on my bare king. So I cash in the exchange now.

Black's bishop on h4 is free, and I prefer taking with the queen because then Qh4 and Rf1 both hit the loose knight on f2 while my knight stays on f3 covering d2 and g5 (after Nxh4 instead, Black gets ...Ne4 with the nasty ...Nd2+ fork). The knight on f2 has no good square: ...Nd3 runs into cxd3, ...Nh3 or ...Ng4 drops to the queen/knight, so I win material.

My knight on f2 is attacked by Rf1 and undefended, and almost every retreat (d1, h1 to the rook; d3 to c2; h3, g4... ) drops it — but Ne4 is defended by the f5 pawn (Qxe4 fxe4 wins the queen), so it's the one safe square. From e4 the knight also covers g5 and g3, so Qg5+ runs into Nxg5, Qf6 into Nxf6, and Qd8+ into Rxd8, meaning White has no immediate check or capture that wins material.

Black's knight on e4 is threatening Nd2+ followed by Nxf1 (and also Rxf3 gxf3 Nd2+ with the same idea), so I must cover the d2 square while keeping d4 protected. Rd1 does both: after Nd2+ Rxd2 simply wins the knight, Nf2 drops to Qxf2, and I keep my queen plus extra pawn advantage with pressure on the loose knight on d7.

My knight on e4 was simply hanging to Qxe4, and my knight on d7 was also loose, so 24...Ndf6 solves both at once — the f6 knight defends e4, the e4 knight defends f6, and together they cover g5 (killing the Qg5+ ideas) plus hit h5 and g4. I checked that 25.Qxf6 Nxf6 wins the queen and that 25.Qf4 or 25.Ng5 only regains the f5 pawn while my knights stay mutually protected.

Black's knights on e4 and f6 defend each other, so capturing either just loses my queen for a piece; instead I noticed the f5 pawn is completely undefended (the f7 pawn blocks the rook). Qf4 hits f5 and e4 at once, and Black has no good way to hold f5 — knight retreats like Nd6 or Nd5 just lose material to Qxf6/Qxf5 forking.

Qf4 hits my Ne4 (defended only by Nf6) and, more importantly, the loose f5 pawn, so I listed every knight move: Nd5 or Nd7 abandon e4 (Qxe4 wins a piece), Nc3+/Nd2+ just drop a knight to bxc3/Rxd2, and Nxh5 lets Qxf5 fork both knights. Nd6 moves the attacked knight to safety while defending f5, keeping my material count intact.

review.label: inaccuracy
review.refutation: 26. Qg5+ Kh7 27. Qxf6 Rg8 28. Qxd6 b5

moves.thought: I checked whether the knight on d6 is defended — the c-pawn is on c6, Nf6 doesn't cover d6, and neither rook reaches d6 with Rf8 blocking the 8th rank, so it's hanging. After Qxd6 Rfd8 I simply retreat with Qf4, and 26...Ne4 27. Qe5 traps that knight too, so I win a clean piece.

I'm down queen-for-rook, so I need material and activity: Nxh5 grabs White's advanced pawn, and I checked no White piece attacks h5 (Qd6, Nf3 and Rd1 all miss it), while after g4 I just reply fxg4 and the knight stays safe. My Rc8 also guards d8, so any queen entry there costs White queen for rook, which keeps my scrappy two-rooks-and-knight counterplay alive.

Note that Qxc6 would simply lose the queen to Rxc6, so I avoid it; instead I centralize with Qd5, which forks the loose b7 and f5 pawns while also eyeing f7 and keeping d4 supported by Rd1. Black's best tries (Nf6 or Nf4 hitting the queen) just let me pick up a pawn with Qxf5 or Qd7, keeping my extra queen-for-rook material.

The queen just landed on d5, but it is completely undefended — my Rd1 check shows White's rook is blocked by its own d4 pawn, and the knight on f3 covers d4/e5, not d5 — so the simple pawn capture cxd5 wins the queen for a pawn. I verified White has no check or counter-capture afterward (Ne5 hits only f7, which Rf8 and the king defend), so I go from down material to up a full rook.

I'm a rook down, so I need activity and material back: Nh4 is safe (Black's knight on h5 doesn't cover h4) and hits the undefended f5 pawn, which Black can't easily defend. The alternatives like Rc1 or c3 are passive and leave me simply a rook behind with no counterplay.

Rxc2 is the trap my first rule warns about — c2 is guarded by Kb1, so that just loses a rook; my real asset is being a full rook up with level pawns. Nf4 keeps the knight active and safe (nothing attacks f4 right now), hits g2 so that if White grabs f5 I take g2 back, and it keeps the option of ...Ng6 to trade knights into a clean two-rooks-vs-rook win.

Material is level, but Black's knight on f4 is the only active piece, so 29.g3 kicks it while defending g2 — after it retreats I pick up f5 (and the knight has no good squares: Ne2 30.Rd2 traps it, Ng6 30.Nxg6 fxg6 31.Rxd5, Nd3 31.cxd3). Compared to 29.Nxf5 Nxg2 this keeps my extra pawn intact.

White's g3 attacks my knight, so it must move, and Ng6 both saves it and offers a one-for-one trade with the loose knight on h4 — after Nxg6 fxg6 I'm still a full rook up (two rooks vs one) and my f-file rook gets an open file. I rejected Nd3 (cxd3) and Ng2 (Nxg2), which simply drop the piece.

I'm down a rook, so I need material and activity: the f5 pawn is actually undefended (the knight on g6 doesn't cover it, and f7 blocks the rook), so Nxf5 wins a free pawn with the knight safe on f5. If Black tries Ne7 to hit it, Nxe7+ comes with check and I can follow with Nxd5, grabbing another pawn.

White's Nf5 threatens Ne7+ forking my king and the c8 rook, so I must cover e7; Rfe8 does it while keeping the c8 rook active on the open c-file, and f7 stays guarded by my king. Ne7 and Rxc2 both just drop a piece (Nxe7+ and Kxc2), so with an extra rook I simply neutralise the knight and keep everything defended.

I'm down a rook, so I need the tactic: my knight on f5 can jump to d6 where it forks both black rooks (c8 and e8), and nothing attacks d6 — the g6 knight doesn't cover it and Re1 isn't check since my rook on d1 blocks the rank. Black's best is something like Rcd8 Nxe8 Rxe8, which wins material back and gets me close to equality.

White's Nd6 forks my rooks but they defend each other, so it's not a real threat; instead I notice d6 is completely undefended (White's Rd1 is blocked by its own d4 pawn), so 31...Rcd8 attacks the knight while keeping d8 protected by my e8 rook. The knight must run, and I stay a whole rook up with my e-file rook free to invade on e2 later.

My knight on d6 is attacked by the rook on d8 and undefended, so I must act; Nxb7 both saves the knight and wins a pawn while simultaneously attacking the d8 rook, forcing Black to retreat (Rd6 loses the rook to Nxd6, and Re2 allows Nxd8). That reduces my deficit to a rook for two pawns, which is a better practical try than Nxe8 Rxe8 giving up the knight for a rook.

My d8 rook is attacked by Nb7, and I must also note Nb7 covers d6, so Rd6?? loses a rook to Nxd6. Rd7 steps off the attacked square, hits the knight, and covers d6 so Nd6 drops the knight to Rxd6; it also keeps f7 guarded while I stay up a rook and a knight.

My knight on b7 is attacked by the rook on d7, so I must move it; Nd6 and Nd8 both lose the piece immediately to the rooks. Nc5 keeps the knight safe while counter-attacking the d7 rook and giving it a strong central outpost (with Ne4/Ne6 ideas), which is better than the passive Na5.

White's Nc5 hits my undefended rook on d7, so I must address it; Ne5 drops to dxe4... dxe5 and Rc7 runs into Nxd5 followed by the Nf6+ fork of king and both rooks. Rde7 keeps the rook safe (defended by Re8), doubles on the open e-file for a later Re2 invasion, and gives White no checks or forks while I stay a full rook up.

I'm down a rook for two pawns, so I need to shore up my second rank and keep pawns while blockading. Rd2 is safe (no black piece attacks d2), guards b2/c2 along the rank, and if Black plays Re1+ I simply step Kb2, after which rook trades on e2/d2 lead toward a knight endgame where my extra pawns give counterplay; moves like Re1, Ne4, Nd7 or Ne6 all just drop the piece outright.

First I checked captures against my knight: Ne5 drops to dxe5 and Nf4/Nh4 drop to gxf4/gxh4, so all knight sorties lose a piece. Instead 34...Re2 attacks the undefended d2 rook from the invaded second rank — White must either trade (35.Rxe2 Rxe2 keeps me a full rook for two pawns with an active rook hitting b2/c2) or retreat, when I keep both rooks and threaten Rxc2; it's a one-for-one trade that never touches my extra piece.

review.label: inaccuracy
review.refutation: 35. Rxe2 Rxe2 36. b4 Ne7 37. a4 Nf5

moves.thought: Black's Re2 both attacks my rook and sets up the deadly back-rank plan Re1+ Rd1 Rxd1#, so moves like Rd1, Rd3 or Nb3 lose on the spot; trading a pair of rooks removes the second attacker. After Rxe2 Rxe2 I can meet the mate threat with a3, giving my king the a2 escape square while my knight stays active.

White's rook on e2 just captured and is completely undefended — the knight on c5 covers d3/e4/e6 but not e2, and the king on b1 is too far. Recounting attackers and defenders as my rule demands, Rxe2 simply wins a whole rook, leaving me R+N+3P against N+5P, and my rook on the second rank also pressures c2.

Black's rook is hitting c2, so I must address that; c3 both saves the pawn (Rxb2+ would just lose the rook to Kxb2) and builds a compact a2-b2-c3-d4 chain that my king and knight can hold. c4 would only lose a pawn to dxc4, and Kc1 is needlessly passive.

I'm up a rook for two pawns, so my priority is keeping everything safe while grabbing the loose g3 pawn — Re4 and Re6 both lose the rook to Nxe4/Nxe6, and Ne5/Nf4/Nh4 drop the knight to dxe5 or gxf3-pawn captures. Re3 is attacked by nothing, hits the undefended g3 pawn and the c3 pawn, and any White attempt to defend with Ne4 or Nd3 simply loses the knight to my rook on the e-file/third rank.

My g3 pawn is hanging to Rxg3 while c3 is safely covered by b2, and knight moves like Ne4 or Nd3 just drop the piece to the rook or the d5 pawn. So I advance the pawn out of the rook's reach with g4, keeping my knight active on c5 and my pawn mass intact.

I'm up a rook for two pawns, so I must avoid the capture-chain traps my notebook warns about: Rxc3 drops the rook to bxc3, Re4/Rd3/Re6 all walk into the c5 knight, and Re5/Ne5 are met by dxe5. Rg3 is completely safe (no white unit reaches g3) and attacks the undefended g4 pawn; if 38.Ne4 then Rxg4 both saves the rook and hits the knight, and 38.Nd7 Rxg4 Nf6+ Kg7 simply loses the knight to my king.

I'm down a rook, so I need active counterplay rather than passive defense; g4 is falling anyway, so instead of defending it I strike at the base of Black's structure with c4, since d5 is undefended and either falls or, after dxc4, my d-pawn becomes a supported passer with the queenside majority. Tactically c4 is safe — Black's only check is Rg1+, which I answer with Kc2.

g4 is completely undefended (Nc5 covers a4/b3/d3/e4/e6/d7/b7/a6, not g4), so Rxg4 grabs a free pawn with no knight fork or check in reply; if White answers cxd5 he gets weak doubled d-pawns and I simply take d4 and then d5, since neither is defended by the knight. Keeping my rook active and munching pawns beats dxc4, which scatters my pawns and gives White a supported passer.

My c4 pawn is hanging to the d5 pawn, and after quiet moves like Nd3 or b4 Black just grabs it with dxc4, so cxd5 both eliminates Black's pawn and leaves me a passed d-pawn to fight with. The Nd7 idea of threatening Nf6+ to win the rook is too easily met (Rg2, Rg1+ or Rg7 all defuse it) while costing me the c-pawn, so I'll take.

The d4 pawn is completely undefended (the knight on c5 covers e4/d3/b3 but not d4), so Rxd4 wins a pawn, kills one of White's connected passers and immediately attacks the loose d5 pawn as well. If White chases with 40.Ne6 or 40.Nb3, I simply take with Rxd5, eliminating the last dangerous passer while keeping my extra rook.

My d5 pawn is attacked and nothing can defend it (Nb3 attacks the rook but Rxd5 both takes the pawn and escapes), so I'd rather push it: d6 creates an advanced passer that Black must respect, and after Rxd6 I regain a tempo with Nb7 or Ne4 hitting the rook. Down material, this passed pawn is my only practical counterplay.

I recounted the defenders of d6: the knight on c5 covers a4/b3/d3/e4/e6/d7/b7/a6 but not d6, so the dangerous passer is completely undefended and Rxd6 simply wins it for free. After Rxd6 White can only harass with Ne4 or Nb7, and my rook steps aside while keeping my extra rook and killing the only real counterplay.

I'm down a rook, so I need activity and tempo-gaining tricks; Nb7 attacks the rook on d6 while staying safe (Nd7 and Ne6 just lose to Rxd7 and fxe6, and Ne4 can be hit by f5). After the rook moves I can keep harassing it from c5/a5 and push my queenside pawns.

My rook on d6 is attacked by Nb7, so it must move; Rd7 steps out of the attack while hitting the undefended knight and simultaneously guarding both a7 and f7, leaving nothing loose. If the knight runs with Nc5 I just play Rd5 to chase it again, and Nd6 simply loses to Rxd6, so my rook-plus-knight material edge stays intact.

My knight on b7 is attacked by the rook on d7, so I must move it; Nd6 and Nd8 both hang to the rook, and Na5 is passive. Nc5 saves the knight with tempo by attacking the rook on d7, and from c5 the knight can later come to d3 to shield my b2 pawn.

White's Nc5 attacks my rook on d7, so I must move it — and Rd5 both saves the rook and attacks the undefended knight on c5 (the knight does not cover d5, and nothing else of White's reaches that square). If the knight runs I keep rook plus knight for nothing; no White check or capture hits anything of mine.

My knight on c5 is attacked by the rook, so I must move it; Nd3, Nd7 and Ne6 all drop it immediately (rook on the d-file, or fxe6). Na6 steps to safety while hitting the a7 pawn, gaining a tempo and giving my last pawns some hope in this lost material situation.

I'm up a rook and a knight, so the main job is to avoid any fork or loose-piece trick while increasing pressure; Ra5 attacks the undefended knight on a6 along the a-file and the fifth rank, and I checked every knight reply — Nc5 and Nb4 just lose the piece to my rook, Nb8/Nc7 leave it hounded, and b4 allows Rxa6. No reply forks my king and rook, and my a7 and f7 pawns stay untouched.

new_lessons: [middlegame] Before any queen or piece move, check every enemy bishop, knight and rook line hitting the destination square; a developed bishop covers squares two files away Example: 13...Qc7?? ran into 14.Bxc7: White's Bf4 already guarded c7, 46%→3%

[middlegame] Before any quiet or developing move, name your loose pieces and list every enemy check and capture on them; if one wins material, choose another move Example: 11.Bc4?? Qh4+ 12.Bf2 Qxc4 with king uncastled, 55%→8%

[middlegame] When a piece is attacked, also weigh pawn moves that counterattack or gain a tempo, and test whether a check first wins your intended retreat square Example: 25...Nd6? lost to 26.Qg5+ Kh7 27.Qxf6 then Qxd6; 25...c5 held

[middlegame] Play every capture chain on a square to the end, recounting attackers and defenders after each trade; a piece never defends the square it moves to Example: ...Qc3 "forked" rooks but bxc3 won the queen; 27...Rf5 was "backed" by the rook that had moved

[middlegame] Before trading a minor piece, play the recapture: if a pawn recapture opens a file or diagonal toward your king or leaves pawns loose, keep the piece Example: 17...Nc4 18.Bxc4 dxc4 opened the e-file for Re4 and left c4 hanging, 51%→9%

[middlegame] Keep a piece on an advanced square only if a pawn can support it; retreat it before enemy pawns take away every escape square Example: Unsupported Ne4 had no retreat after e5/d6; Bd5 and Be4 were chased by pawns

[middlegame] Never push pawns in front of your castled king while an enemy bishop or queen eyes those squares; answer a wing storm with a central break instead Example: 17.g3 invited ...fxg3 and ...Bxh3; 17.dxc6 kept a winning game

[middlegame] When your rook can invade the enemy second rank hitting loose pawns, prefer that to any equal trade; with exposed kings activity beats simplification Example: Instead of 17...Nc4, 17...Rf2 grabbing h2 and tying White down was winning

[endgame] With extra material and rooks on an open file, do not offer the trade to a defended enemy rook; insert a check first and keep both rooks active Example: 34...Re2 allowed 35.Rxe2; 34...Re1+ drove the king back, 98% vs 91%

[endgame] With extra material, trade one-for-one but never your last extra piece; cut off his king, take the 7th rank, and push a pawn only with escort Example: Refusing 31.Rd5 dropped 94%→61%; 59...b5 pushed an unescorted pawn instead of Rd5

[endgame] Keep extra pawns connected, stay inside the square of every passer, and before each move check enemy Kx-captures and stalemate traps Example: 66...Qc3+? Kxc3 drew a won queen endgame; 29...dxc4 scattered a6/c4/c6

[opening] Delay the central break (d5/e5) until minors are developed and the king is castled; when two units can recapture, use the minor piece, not the queen Example: 8...d5 exd5 left a backward pawn, 48%→42%; 10...Qxd5? 11.Qxd5 lost a tempo

[middlegame] After castling opposite wings, spend a tempo on Kb1/Kh1 and lift a rook (Rh4) along a file fixed by your own wing pawn, instead of trading attackers Example: Caro-Kann 8.h5 h6: 13.Kb1 then Rh4 beat 13.Ne4, which swapped off the attack

[middlegame] When a bishop pins your knight against king or a loose rook, kick the pinner with a3/h3 or block with Bd2 rather than defending passively with the queen Example: 12.Qd2 let ...Nc5-e4 pile on; 12.a3 questioned Bb4 at once, 59%→54%
